content.text: The report is a clean regression: on Windows, mise now exposes a generated extensionless `.mise-bins\fnox` file instead of the real `fnox.exe`. I’m tracing what changed between 2026.9.1 and 2026.9.2 and checking whether the same path affects other single-binary tools.

The cause is now clear: Packslip intentionally canonicalizes `fnox.exe` to the command name `fnox`; mise then copies the executable to that extensionless name on Windows. Unix symlinks tolerate that convention, but Windows process discovery requires a `PATHEXT` suffix, so this is a backend-wide Windows bug rather than a bad fnox archive.

content.text:
Confirmed a mise Packslip backend bug on Windows.

- Packslip correctly declares `fnox.exe`, but canonicalizes its command name to `fnox`.
- Mise copies the executable into `.mise-bins` using that canonical name verbatim.
- Unix accepts an extensionless symlink; Windows requires the resulting file to be named `fnox.exe`.
- The regression appeared in v2026.9.2 when [#12845](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12845) switched fnox’s preferred backend from `github:` to `packslip:`. The underlying linking behavior came from [#12778](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12778).
- v2026.9.3 and current `main` remain affected.

The correct fix is narrowly scoped: when linking Packslip executables on Windows, append `.exe` to the canonical PATH name. This follows Packslip’s explicit contract; the fnox manifest and registry entry are not faulty.

Potentially affected Windows shorthands are `aube`, `communique`, `fnox`, `hk`, `mr-boxington`, `pitchfork`, and `usage` at versions using Packslip.

Immediate workaround:

```powershell
mise use -g github:jdx/fnox@1.35.1
```

A fix should include a Windows unit test for `.mise-bins\fnox.exe` and a Pester regression that actually executes the command. No files were changed during this investigation.
